output.title: Rollback drills should start at the approval boundary
output.body:
If you are rethinking rollback drills, the useful question is not “can we roll back?” It is: when a pilot automation does the wrong thing, who notices first, and what can they stop without waiting on anyone else?

For a small business, I would treat rollback as a workflow decision, not a technical slogan. Bareni’s operating model keeps the customer’s database, automation-tool, and API accounts in the customer’s name from day one, with finished code handed over. That is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not a legal warranty, but it does point to the right control: the owner should be able to pause, change, or disable the workflow in their own environment.

Keep one line non-negotiable: anything that moves money or makes another high-risk decision stays under human approval. No exceptions, no clever detours, no “the agent said it was fine.”

The practical next step is simple. Pick one recurring workflow and write down the approval boundary before you build: what must always stay human, what can be automated, and who checks the output if it looks off. If that boundary is unclear, the rollback drill is really a design problem. Better to find that out on paper than after the polite little machine has made itself too comfortable.
